questions.q: Define capacitance and state its SI unit. Write the formula relating charge, potential difference, and capacitance.
questions.a: Capacitance \(C\) is the ratio of the magnitude of charge \(Q\) on one conductor to the potential difference \(V\) between the two conductors: \(C = Q/V\). The SI unit is the farad (F), where \(1 \text{ F} = 1 \text{ C/V}\). A wrong answer (e.g., "capacitance is the charge stored" or unit "coulomb") reveals the student confuses the stored charge \(Q\) with the capacity \(C\) to hold that charge per volt.

questions.q: A student says: "If I double the charge on a capacitor, its capacitance doubles because \(C = Q/V\)." Explain why this reasoning is incorrect. What actually happens to \(V\) when \(Q\) is doubled?
questions.a: The reasoning is incorrect because \(C\) is a geometric constant for a given capacitor; it does not depend on \(Q\) or \(V\). From \(C = Q/V\), if \(Q\) is doubled, \(V\) also doubles (since \(V \propto Q\) for a fixed geometry), keeping \(C\) unchanged. A wrong answer (e.g., "V stays the same" or "C doubles") reveals the student treats the formula as a simple algebraic relation without understanding the physical proportionality \(Q \propto V\) implied by Coulomb's law and superposition.

questions.q: A capacitor has a capacitance of \(5.0 \text{ nF}\). When connected to a \(12 \text{ V}\) battery, what is the magnitude of charge on each plate? If the same capacitor is instead connected to a \(6.0 \text{ V}\) battery, what is the new charge? Show unit analysis.
questions.a:
Given \(C = 5.0 \text{ nF} = 5.0 \times 10^{-9} \text{ F}\).
Case 1: \(V = 12 \text{ V}\). \(Q = C V = (5.0 \times 10^{-9} \text{ F}) \times (12 \text{ V}) = 6.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C} = 60 \text{ nC}\).
Case 2: \(V = 6.0 \text{ V}\). \(Q = (5.0 \times 10^{-9}) \times 6.0 = 3.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C} = 30 \text{ nC}\).
Unit analysis: \(\text{F} \times \text{V} = (\text{C/V}) \times \text{V} = \text{C}\). A wrong answer (e.g., forgetting to convert nF to F, or getting 60 C) reveals unit conversion errors or misunderstanding that \(Q\) scales linearly with \(V\).

questions.q: Two identical parallel-plate capacitors are built. Capacitor A has air between plates; Capacitor B has a dielectric with constant \(K = 4\) filling the space. Both are given the same charge \(Q\). Compare their potential differences \(V_A\) and \(V_B\). Which capacitor has higher capacitance?
questions.a: Since \(C = Q/V\) and \(Q\) is the same, \(V \propto 1/C\). The dielectric increases capacitance by factor \(K\): \(C_B = K C_A = 4 C_A\). Therefore \(V_B = V_A / 4\). Capacitor B has higher capacitance (4 times) and lower potential difference (1/4) for the same charge. A wrong answer (e.g., "V_B = V_A" or "C_B = C_A") reveals the student does not grasp that dielectric reduces the effective field for the same free charge, thus reducing \(V\) and increasing \(C\).

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "A single isolated metal sphere cannot have capacitance because a capacitor requires two conductors." Is this true or false? Justify your answer using the definition of capacitance and the concept of potential at infinity.
questions.a: False. A single isolated conductor can be treated as a capacitor with the second conductor at infinity (where potential is defined as zero). The capacitance of an isolated sphere of radius \(R\) is \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R\). The definition \(C = Q/V\) still holds, where \(V\) is the potential of the sphere relative to infinity. A wrong answer ("true") reveals the student thinks capacitance strictly requires two physical plates, missing the conceptual extension to infinity used in electrostatics.

questions.q: Design a simple capacitor using household materials (aluminum foil, paper, plastic wrap) that can store enough charge to light a small LED briefly when discharged. Describe how you would increase its capacitance without changing the materials.
questions.a: A good answer: Use two sheets of aluminum foil separated by paper (dielectric). Roll them into a cylinder to increase effective area \(A\) and decrease separation \(d\) (thin paper). Capacitance \(C \propto A/d\). To increase \(C\) without new materials: (1) use larger foil sheets (increase \(A\)), (2) use thinner paper (decrease \(d\)), (3) add more layers (effectively parallel combination). A poor answer (e.g., "add more charge" or "use a higher voltage battery") reveals confusion between changing \(C\) (geometry) vs changing \(Q\) or \(V\).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A capacitor is a system of two ______ separated by an insulating medium (or vacuum) that stores electric charge and energy.
Fill in the blank: Observe a ceiling fan in your home — it has a small ______ component (a capacitor) that helps the motor start.
